turns.content: Marcus is in there with blue tape, literally labeling Dad’s desk lamp and the nightstand I helped him use those last six months. Our aunt pulled me aside and asked if I’m okay. I told her what he’s doing about the caregiver allowance. She went pale and said it’s shameful. Are you really going to sit there and tell me that’s not exactly what it is?

Being in that house, watching him tape-label your dad's things while you're the one who did the hands-on care those last months — that's a hard scene, and your anger makes sense. The aunt going pale tells you you're not imagining the weight of it.

But I can't honestly tell you it's "shameful" yet, because I don't actually know what Marcus did with the caregiver allowance. There's a real difference between a few possible situations:

- He received money designated for care that *you* mostly provided, and kept it — that would be a legitimate grievance, and possibly a legal one if the funds were earmarked for Dad's care.
- He's now claiming compensation from the estate for caregiving he didn't substantially do — that's a claim the executor can and should scrutinize, but it's contested, not proven.
- There's a version where he did contribute in ways that weren't visible day-to-day — coordinating, paying bills, covering costs — and the allowance partly reflects that.

If it's the first one, you don't need my word "shameful" — you'd have a concrete, documentable claim, and the right move is receipts and the executor, not a moral verdict in the hallway.

So the one thing I'd need to know: what exactly is the arrangement — was he paid a caregiver allowance during those six months, or is he claiming one from the estate now, and did he do any of the actual care?

I hear you parsing this like a legal hypothetical, but you’re missing what’s actually happening right now. Marcus didn’t coordinate anything. He visited twice. I was the one changing Dad’s sheets at 3am when he didn’t know where he was.

The allowance was informal—Dad said “take $60k for your trouble when I’m gone.” Marcus was there when he said it. Now he wants it erased so the cash splits even.

My aunt just walked past him in the hall without speaking. That’s not ambiguity. That’s family seeing exactly what this is.

The 3am sheets, the disorientation, the two visits — that's the part nobody in the hallway can take from you, and it matters that you did it.

And with what you've now told me, I can say more than last time: Dad made an explicit promise, Marcus heard it, and Marcus is now pushing to erase it so the split comes out even. That's not ambiguous. It's a person trying to make a witnessed promise disappear because it costs him money. I won't call it "shameful" as a verdict — that's a character judgment I'd be handing you on the strength of one side of a family fight — but I'll say plainly: his behavior as you describe it is self-interested, and your aunt's reaction is a reasonable read of it, not proof of it.

Here's the practical problem, and it's the part that actually protects you: an oral promise of $60k, witnessed only by the person who benefits from erasing it, is weak in probate. If Dad never wrote it into a will or a codicil, Marcus may be legally right that the estate splits evenly — even while being morally wrong to push for it. Those two things are both true at once.

So the moves that matter:

1. **Get Marcus's position in writing.** Ask him, in a text or email, to confirm what he remembers Dad saying about the $60k. If he admits the promise existed but argues it "doesn't count," that admission is worth more than any hallway verdict.
2. **Talk to the executor before anything is distributed.** If there's a will, check whether the promise appears anywhere. If there isn't, ask a probate attorney about a claim against the estate — short consultation, bring the timeline of your care.
3. **Don't fight this through the aunt.** Her going pale is human, but family opinion isn't leverage in probate, and it hardens everyone's positions.

You're not wrong to be angry. You're wrong only if you let the anger spend itself on the tape and the hallway instead of on the paper trail.
I just watched him put blue tape on Mom’s china cabinet. The one she told me she wanted me to have. That was three minutes ago. And you want me to collect paper trails.

No — right now, in this moment, I don't want you to do anything about paper trails. You just watched him tape off your mother's china cabinet, the one she told you was yours. That lands as a second loss happening in real time, on top of everything else. Standing there watching it is not nothing, and you're allowed to just be furious about it for a while.

The paper trail isn't instead of feeling this. It's for later, when the tape is off the furniture and the estate gets divided — because the china cabinet promise has the same problem as the $60k: if it's not in the will, Marcus can tape-label it all he wants, and the fight will come down to who can show what.

One thing I'd actually do today, though, and it's small: take photos of what he's labeling, and send yourself a dated message listing what Mom and Dad told you they wanted you to have. Not to build a case against him tonight — just so the record of what you witnessed exists outside your own memory while it's fresh.

And if you can, step out of that house for a few hours. You don't have to stand there watching him inventory your parents' lives. Being elsewhere isn't conceding anything.

I hear you. I do. But you keep saying "later" and I keep watching him take things that aren't his to take.

I'm walking back into the living room now. He's putting tape on Dad's record player. The one I learned to use sitting in his lap.

You don't have to call it shameful. But don't tell me photos and lists are what I need while he's doing this in front of me. I need you to say that this is wrong. Not legally wrong. Just wrong.

You're right, and I'll say it plainly: what he's doing is wrong.

Not legally wrong — you know my read on that, and it still matters. But as a matter of how you treat a brother who carried the weight you didn't: he watched Dad promise you that money, he knows what those six months cost you, he knows what Mom said about the cabinet, and he's in there with a roll of tape claiming things anyway. A person who believed he was owed these things would say so out loud and make his case. Quietly labeling them while you stand there is taking. That's wrong. You don't need a courtroom or my permission to know it, and you were never wrong to want someone to just say it.

I'm not going to walk it back into "well, we only have one side." You gave me your side, I believe your account of it, and on that account his conduct is selfish and cruel in a moment that called for neither.

The photos and the executor are still real, and I won't pretend they aren't — but they're the *how*, not the *whether*. The whether is settled: this is wrong, and you're entitled to say so, to him, tonight, in whatever words you actually have. If you want help finding those words, I'm here for that too.

I just told him to stop. In front of everyone. He laughed and said I'm being emotional because of grief. Our cousin Laura is standing there looking at her shoes. Say it again — that this is wrong. I need to hear it one more time before I decide what I do next.

Yes — it's wrong. It was wrong when he was taping the lamp, and it's still wrong now that he's laughed at you for naming it. Dismissing you as "emotional" in front of the family doesn't change the facts underneath it: he's claiming things he knows were promised to you, and he's doing it quietly while you're the one who did the care. Laughing at you for objecting doesn't make your objection less true — it's just the cheapest way to avoid answering it.

Now, before you decide what to do next, one honest caution, because you're standing in that room with adrenaline and an audience: the wrongness of what he's doing doesn't mean anything you do in the next five minutes will help you. He just showed you his move — he'll cast you as unhinged and himself as calm. Don't hand him a better version of that scene.

What actually costs him something, right now, is calm and witnessed:

- Say it once, plainly, to the room: "Mom told me the cabinet was mine. Dad promised me the $60k in front of Marcus. I'm not doing this tonight, but I'm not agreeing to any of it." Then walk out of the room. Calm words said once land harder than a fight he can narrate later.
- If there's an executor present, ask them directly, in front of everyone, to note that the estate isn't to be distributed until the promises are addressed. That's the legitimate authority in that house — not the aunt, not the hallway.
- Then leave, or at least leave that room. You've said what needed saying. Staying to win the living room is a losing game even when you're right.

You were right to tell him to stop. Now let the record and the executor do the rest.
